item.title: Every Way a Tenant Escaped: A Cross-Tenant Breakout Field Guide
item.description: ePHPm can serve a directory full of sites out of one process. Point sites_dir at a folder, every subdirectory is a virtual host, and the Host header decides which one you get. That’s how the PR preview environment runs: every pull request gets a subdomain, and the code behind it is whatever somebody pushed. One process holding many tenants means every per-tenant boundary is something ePHPm enforces itself, in-process. There’s no container wall between site A and site B unless you add one.

item.title: We Disabled PHP's Stack Guard Ourselves: Containing Segfaults in a Single-Process PHP Server
item.description:
php-fpm has a property nobody thinks about until they leave it: when a worker segfaults, you lose one request. The master forks a new child and life goes on. ePHPm runs every tenant’s PHP as threads inside one process. That’s where the memory and latency wins come from, and it also means one tenant’s segfault takes down every other tenant on the box.

This is the story of closing that gap, in four steps over about two weeks. The last step turned out to be a bug we’d put there ourselves. It’s also the payoff for the thread pool work in the previous post: everything below that actually shipped depends on ePHPm owning its own PHP threads.

item.title: Per-Tenant Network Policy in One Process: ePHPm's eBPF Thread Tags
item.description:
In multi-tenant mode ePHPm serves every site in sites_dir from one process. Every tenant’s PHP runs as the same OS user, on the same pool of ZTS threads, and a thread that just served blog.example will serve shop.example a few milliseconds later. That’s the density win. It also means the kernel has no idea which tenant is behind a given connect(). As far as Linux is concerned it’s all ephpm-web.

Most of the isolation work in ePHPm happens above the kernel: open_basedir, the function denylist, per-site databases and KV keyspaces. Network is the one place where that isn’t enough. This week we brought eBPF in to give the kernel a per-tenant identity. It went from a roadmap doc on Wednesday morning to merged that evening (#413, aimed at v0.8.1). v0.8.1 never got a release because its Linux legs failed to link. v0.8.2 shipped with the BPF object silently stubbed out, and v0.8.3 was the first release that actually carried it. This post covers what it enforces, what it costs, what broke on the way out the door, and what it doesn’t do.
